#2093. “Welcome Back” Paco On The Market Following Dismissal | West Ham News

Former West Ham assistant coach Paco Jémez is once again searching for a new club after being relieved of his duties by Moroccan giants Raja Casablanca following a disappointing start to the season.

Jémez earned admirers for the attacking brand of football he implemented in Spain, and many supporters pointed to the turnaround in performances at West Ham as being credited to him.

However, his latest managerial venture has come to an abrupt end after Raja Casablanca opted to make a change just over two months after appointing him.

The club confirmed that Sunday’s 2-0 defeat to RS Berkane would be Jémez’s final match in charge, with officials deciding a fresh approach was needed after reviewing the team’s performances and results.

An official club statement explained that the sporting management felt a change in technical leadership was necessary to provide a new dynamic and improve the club’s chances of meeting its objectives this season.

Despite arriving in Casablanca with an impressive CV that included spells at Rayo Vallecano, Granada, Las Palmas and Mexican side Cruz Azul, the Spaniard struggled to generate momentum. Raja collected just six points from their opening five league fixtures, winning once, drawing three times and losing once.

Those results left his new club down in 13th place and under growing pressure, a situation made worse by a run of performances that failed to convince supporters.

Reports in Morocco had suggested Jémez’s future was already under scrutiny before the defeat against Berkane, with the coach reportedly asking club officials for more time to improve results. However, the latest setback proved decisive.

Following the defeat, Jémez accepted responsibility and apologised to supporters, acknowledging that the team had not produced the level of performance expected from one of Morocco’s biggest clubs. He also stated that he would accept whatever decision the board deemed appropriate.

West Ham ultimately went in a different direction by appointing Rui Pedro Silva as assistant head coach in the summer, despite Jémez publicly stating he wanted to stay on. Yet as of this morning, things have moved on!

Jémez’s latest dismissal serves as a reminder of the ruthless nature of football management.

A coach once regarded as one of Spain’s most innovative tacticians now finds himself looking for a fresh opportunity after another short-lived spell in the dugout.

#2092. Newcastle 0 Everton 1 match ratings and comments on all the Newcastle United players

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 0 Everton 1 in the Premier League.

I’m writing this the morning after the game; I was far too cheesed off last night to type anything sensible. To be honest, my mood has not really changed.

Newcastle were deservedly beaten by an Everton side that are everything Newcastle are not; well-organised, clear in their gameplan, and confident in their team mates.

For most of the game, Newcastle showed all the characteristics of a team low on confidence: clearances hurried, crosses punted out of play, passes rushed and going straight to a blue. The one thing that we did well was play some slick passes in areas that were never going to hurt Everton, and Everton were happy to let us do that.

We had a couple of spells in the game when things looked a little more hopeful, but in truth we only looked good when the subs came on; in fact the more subs we brought on, the better we looked. I think I’m correct in saying that it was added time before we had a shot on target, and that is just not good enough.

There will be those who say Everton’s goal should not have stood, because Barry put an arm into Schär’s face, but I watched the incident back, and for me, it was one of those 50:50 incidents that you sometimes get and sometimes don’t. The real reason Everton scored was atrocious defending. And if some Geordies say we should have had a penalty for a foul on Lewis Hall, then (a) I disagree, and (b) Everton should definitely have had one when Schär upended Barry.

I got the feeling that the crowd turned last night, or at least started to. At full time – despite Newcastle’s late rally – the mood was reminiscent of the dark days of McClaren and Bruce. Fans are running out of patience with the manager and the team. Personally, I’d stick with Jaissle and give him time, but I understand those who are ready to see him go.

I don’t believe we’ll be in a relegation scrap but nor do I believe we’ll be troubling any teams outside of England next season. We would have gone seventh (net 6th if Manchester City receive the expected points deduction) if we’d won last night. Instead, a team with limited ambitions vaulted above us into that position. And deserved to.

Lukáš Horníček 4 Actually made a couple of good saves second half, but only after he allowed the ball to squirm under his body to the feet of a grateful Thierno Barry, who could not miss.

Amar Dedić 4 Had a couple of runs upfield but didn’t know what to do when he got there. Other than that, I don’t remember him doing much at all. I don’t know enough about football to say that he was complicit in the poor defending that led to Everton’s goal but it wasn’t a good look.

Fabian Schär 4 Went down too easily when Barry scored, hoping to win a free kick. Didn’t get it. Could easily have conceded a pen when he took the legs of the same player. He looked out of sorts. His passing – usually a strength – was poor.

Dan Burn 6 Showed tenacity, desire and leadership when others showed none of those things. Wasn’t immune to a bit of panicking but not as much as some of his colleagues.

Lewis Hall 6 OK overall. At least he tried. By the end of the game, he was playing almost as a midfielder trying to get things going.

Nico Gonzàlez 3 His poorest game for us. No presence, no authority, and displaying a lack of belief that spread through the team. If he’d come from Stoke City on a free, you’d say he wasn’t good enough on this form.

Joelinton 5 I see him getting pelters in some quarters today but I thought he was a lot better than Nico. Tried to initiate some attacks and looked more interested than most. He didn’t have a great game but at least he didn’t hide.

Anthony Elanga 3 Elanga is back to the version we saw last season. Creates very little, loses the ball too easily, looks ordinary. And completely failed to track Tyrique George as he sauntered into our area to set up Everton’s goal. He was meant to be an upgrade on Murphy, and apart from a couple of times, he’s never really looked like it.

Joe Willock 4 Started quite brightly compared to many, but began to fade, and then kept fading.

Harvey Barnes 5 Kept going. Showed a willingness to get on the ball and attack our opponents more than most. Not a great game. If he had been taking an exam, he’d get a pass mark, but no more.

William Osula 5 He doesn’t lack enthusiasm and that is a good thing. What he lacked last night was service and awareness. Made the wrong runs a few times and made the wrong decision on others. That he hardly saw the ball was not all his fault.

Sean Steur 7 Our Player of the Match and he was only on for half an hour.

Instantly improved our attacking options, playing passes through the Everton defence, and showing a composure that those with a decade more experience did not. I guess the manager wants to protect him, given our current plight and Steur’s tender years, but he is a baller, and he needs to start. If not now, when?

Yoane Wissa 4 Well, he had – I think – our first and second shots on target, but he fluffed his lines. I have some sympathy for Wissa – against a side like Everton, who packed the area at 1-0, and whose defenders are massive, a small, quick striker like him is always going to be at a disadvantage. But he needs to improve his shooting.

Jacob Ramsey 2 I thought he looked pretty good when he joined the fray. Positive, combative and determined. I thought he’d scored at one point – my arms were in the air – but it whistled past the post. 10 minutes later he was in the shower after two yellows in almost record time. The second one – which could have been a red – was inexcusable. It just capped off an awful night.

Jacob Murphy 5 Didn’t stand out, but was better than many of his team mates, including the player he replaced. Kept the Everton defence interested.

Bazoumana Touré 6 I know he ‘wasn’t on long enough to judge’ but he looked better than just about everyone bar Steur.

Livened up the team, livened up the crowd. If I was Jaissle, I’d throw caution to the wind and start him and Steur. Our regular starters look jaded.

#2090. Ruthless Křetínský Refuses To Gamble His West Ham Reputation On Nuno Any Longer

Daniel Křetínský has demonstrated that there is a limit to how far he is prepared to gamble his reputation at West Ham United on Nuno Espírito Santo. Having backed the Portuguese coach during the summer, the Czech billionaire has now seen the club abandon that decision following a disappointing start to the Championship campaign.

It represents a significant change of direction for West Ham, particularly given the circumstances surrounding Nuno’s retention after relegation. David Sullivan had reportedly favoured a managerial change, but Křetínský supported the idea of continuity and giving the existing head coach an opportunity to lead the promotion campaign.

At the time, I could understand the argument, even if I wasn’t convinced by it. But following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion, West Ham’s board has now decided that the situation cannot continue.

There was always an element of risk attached to retaining Nuno following relegation.

He had failed to keep West Ham in the Premier League, but the argument for keeping him was that he knew the squad, understood the club and could provide the stability needed for an immediate return.

Unfortunately, that stability never really materialised.

West Ham have spent much of the Championship campaign struggling to establish a recognisable playing style, with the manager regularly changing formations and personnel.

And despite the considerable talent available to him, Nuno appeared increasingly unable to get the best out of his players.

The 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion was particularly damaging because it exposed so many of the problems supporters had been highlighting for months.

The team looked disorganised, short of confidence and heavily reliant on Jarrod Bowen to produce something out of nothing.

It was hardly the performance of a side looking capable of securing automatic promotion.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer

The decision to retain Nuno was never simply about the manager.

West Ham had already committed themselves to a huge financial gamble following relegation, selling a substantial amount of their most valuable talent while attempting to rebuild a squad capable of returning to the Premier League.

There was an understandable desire to reduce costs, but also an expectation that the club would use its remaining resources wisely.

And that is where Nuno’s continued struggles became particularly worrying.

Having sold so much of the family silver during the summer, West Ham cannot simply assume they will get another opportunity to flex their financial muscle in the Championship.

A second season outside the Premier League could present an entirely different challenge.

The club needs good coaching, sensible recruitment and a clear tactical identity.

As Nils Koppen’s plans for a recognisable West Ham footballing identity demonstrated, there is already an ambition to establish something more sustainable.

But that was becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the football being produced under Nuno.

What I found particularly interesting when researching Křetínský’s history at Sparta Prague was his willingness to change managers when a club’s objectives appeared to be under threat.

At Sparta, those objectives generally involved winning titles or securing Champions League football.

At West Ham, the immediate equivalent is automatic promotion.

I had previously assumed that because Křetínský backed Nuno during the summer, he would be reluctant to abandon that decision.

His Sparta record made me reconsider that assumption.

Of course, we should distinguish the board’s collective decision from any suggestion that Křetínský personally ordered Nuno’s dismissal. The club has not publicly established who drove the final decision.

Nevertheless, the outcome is clear. The manager Křetínský reportedly wanted to retain is no longer in charge.

Křetínský’s reputation will not ultimately be judged on whether he supported Nuno for a few months too long.

It will be judged on whether West Ham can get back into the Premier League.

And having taken the decision to change managers, the board now has to ensure the next appointment gives the club the best possible opportunity to achieve that objective.

There is still plenty of talent in this squad, and I remain convinced a better-organised team could produce considerably more convincing performances.

West Ham have made their decision. Now they need to make sure it was worth making.

Watching the latest Newcastle United match against Everton on TV, I turned to the missus after 10 minutes and said: “We’re not gonna win this one.”

My verdict was less than insightful; anyone inside St James’ Park on Monday night would have quickly realised the visitors looked the better team and were seemingly playing with an extra man, such was their early control.

Matthais Jassle fronted up in post-match interviews but there was little comfort in his words. “It’s not easy to explain as it looked so good during the week [in training]. The lads looked committed and the confidence was there. Today from the start the confidence was missing. We need to improve really fast. We have to encourage them that they are able to do it, that they have the potential to play in that way.”

The task of restoring confidence is a tough gig for any manager, never mind one whose experience of coaching in the Premier League was as comprehensive as mine only three months ago.

Apart from the encounters with an undercooked Liverpool and a hapless Tottenham, there have been only glimpses of “the Jaissle way” this season. We started like thoroughbreds against the previously unbeaten Hull City, then ran out of energy. We blew away Crystal Palace in the 15 minutes immediately after the interval at a windswept Selhurst Park, having produced a first half of dire quality.

The head coach says he sees the players do it in training. That’s worth diddly squat once they cross the white line and are confronted not by their mates but by opponents determined to make us second best. Everton have done it twice, so have Villa, Coventry and Leeds United.

Time for a history lesson. In the mid-70s, the Mackems bought a young winger called Tom Finney. No, not the Preston plumber. This one was a Northern Irishman who played a total of 15 games at Joker Park before leaving for Cambridge United, whom he served with distinction, scoring 56 times in 268 appearances.

So what’s all that got to do with the price of fish? Well, Finney was the subject of an article in the Chronicle by Len Hetherington (the Sunderland version of the great John Gibson) in which the footballer was described as having every quality needed to be a big success. There was just one problem: those abundant skills were seen every time he trained but come match day he was deeply underwhelming.

Which reminds me of an oft-cited quote by the baseball legend Yogi Berra: “Ninety per cent of the game is half-mental.” Even those who struggle with maths should be able to get the drift. An awful lot of competitive sport is played in the head. There’s little difference between confidence and belief. They are almost synonyms. Our German coach says the players are lacking confidence. I suspect belief is the missing ingredient: the players are struggling to believe he is the answer to the question set when Eddie Howe walked away.

Jaissle is 38, with a cv showing success in the Austrian league and in Saudi Arabia. The latter is regarded by most football fans as a vanity project by the Saudi Arabia PIF (who just happen to be the majority owners of Newcastle United). I have not watched even one minute of action, despite the dubious attraction of the preening Portuguese poster boy. My bad!

As for the Austrian League, 11 years ago I found myself in that country’s fascinating capital city. A bit of essential research told me the Prater Park (where the big wheel featured in The Third Man, a 1949 film noir, still slowly turns) was home to Rapid Vienna. They had been runners-up to Red Bull Salzburg in the 2014-15 league. They were top of the table. They were hosting one of their biggest rivals, so what’s a football follower to do?

Leaving Lady R to explore the many other attractions of the area, I headed for the stadium.

The match was dreadful, almost as bad as the first half at Palace last month. The fans spent much of the afternoon goading each other rather than watching the ball, a response quite understandable because of the quality , or lack of, on show. No attempts on target from either side until I broke the habit of a lifetime and walked out with five minutes left. Inevitably, the hosts, whom I had already renamed Vapid Vienna, scored a late, late winner.

For the record, Red Bull Salzburg won the Austrian Bundesliga title for 10 consecutive seasons from 2014, including two when the head coach was Herr Jaissle. That gives some perspective to his achievements.

The other highlight of that day (apart from a failed rendezvous blamed on the presence of a second big wheel in the Prater Park and confusion over Central European Time) was a conversation with the hotel receptionist.

When I asked if she was a fan and said I had just been to watch the league leaders, she looked bemused. “Yes, I am, but not of Austrian football. Why did you go? It’s rubbish.”

OK, that was only one match and the opinion of only one local . . . but maybe she was spot-on. The lesser-known Bundesliga is a long way down the pecking order of Uefa competitions.

Hiring a manager who won two titles there is clearly better than hiring a manager without any honours. Are his medals enough to convince battle-hardened Premier League players, though? The evidence so far suggests that question has not been answered in the affirmative.

We all know there are explanations for the bumps in the road. Our best players sold, even if at least two of them were not at their best last season. Raw young recruits brought in as replacements, though Hornicek, Dedic and Gonzalez were the only summer signings in last night’s line-up. All three are experienced compared with Steur and Toure, who outshone all their teammates despite playing cameo roles.

What is the biggest, most relevant explanation? A lot of supporters are looking no further than the head coach.

Jamie Smith’s excellent match report paints a picture of woe that is difficult to dispute. I’ll be at Craven Cottage on Saturday for a non-televised, 3pm traditional kick-off, thanks to a person who knows a person who has a spare ticket.

Perhaps my first appearance in the away end at Fulham for 47 seasons will bring United a change of fortune.

Until then, there’s a catchily annoying song flying around my brain like a moth trapped in old Mother Hubbard’s cupboard. The seemingly endless summer has finally given way to autumn storms in West Sussex. There’s a chill in the morning air. Twenty months on from the greatest day in the club’s modern history, all I can hear is James Dean Bradfield singing: “You stole the sun from my heart.”

At least he adds: “I love you all the same.”

#2087. Ex-Celtic star’s £22m move takes fresh twist as manager who signed him axed

Arne Engels faces a fresh period of uncertainty at West Ham after the club sacked Nuno Espirito Santo just months after his £22 million move from Celtic.

The former Hoops midfielder has started every Championship game since making the switch to the London Stadium, with Nuno having been a major backer of the Belgian.

Club statement. Read more: https://t.co/LT0TZXbSpR https://t.co/0r6Yz55iRi

— West Ham United (@WestHam) November 3, 2026

But West Ham have now decided to make a change following back-to-back home defeats, leaving the club eighth in the Championship.

Saturday’s 3-1 loss to West Brom prompted what the Hammers described as a “thorough review” of their start to life in the second tier.

The club had opted to stick with Nuno in May despite his failure to preserve their Premier League status, but the Portuguese coach has now been removed from his position.

The managerial change provides an intriguing twist for Arne Engels, who only left Celtic for West Ham in August.

The Belgian made the move in a £22m deal after Celtic rejected two earlier bids, with Martin O’Neill admitting at the time that Engels wanted the transfer and did not want to risk injury by playing in the Hoops’ Champions League play-off.

Martin O’Neill also described the midfielder’s departure as “disappointing” and conceded his running power would be difficult for Celtic to replace.

The ‘biggest trick’ Celtic missed that could come back to haunt them

Rangers-daft pundit sounds Celtic alarm with ‘Covid year’ warning

Celtic's tactics under Martin O'Neill torn apart as ‘biggest pet hate’ laid bare

Arne Engels has since been a regular under Nuno, starting every league match following his arrival, but will now have to impress whoever takes charge next.

West Ham said: “West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team head coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

“Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.

“Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also departed.

“West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

“The process of recruiting a new head coach is already underway.”

Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of preparations for Wednesday night’s Championship trip to Cardiff City.

#2085. Richarlison grabs last-gasp winner for 10-man Spurs in fiery Chelsea friendly

Tottenham concluded their tour Down Under with a 2-1 victory over London rivals Chelsea at Accor Stadium in Sydney.

Sandro Tonali put Tottenham in front with a deflected effort before Estêvão equalised for Chelsea minutes later. Tottenham’s cause was not helped by a red card for Austrian defender Kevin Danso, who lasted just three minutes after coming on at half-time.

After making a mistake, Danso brought João Pedro down and was given his marching orders for denying a clear goal-scoring opportunity. Chelsea came close to taking the lead with their one-man advantage only for Tottenham goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky to make some crucial saves.Just as the game appeared to be heading to penalties, Richarlison scored on the follow-up after Jamie Donley hit the post in the final few seconds of added time.

Richarlison. 90+2. pic.twitter.com/VIOS4Jh7P2

Tottenham will take on Getafe and Hoffenheim back on home soil before taking on Brentford on the opening weekend of the new Premier League season.

Chelsea have four more pre-season games, including fixtures against Juventus and AC Milan, before travelling to Fulham in the opening Premier League game of the Xabi Alonso era.

Chelsea Sharman-Lowe, Palestra, Colwill (Acheampong, 80), Palmer (Kellyman, 80), Gittens (Tosin), Essugo (Walsh, 80), Pedro (Delap, 80), Hato (Anselmino, 62), Fofana (Sarr, 80), Estêvão (Satpayev, 70), Lavia (Nicoll-Jazuli, 46).Substitutes not used Watson, Curd, Subuloye, Emenalo, Kavuma-McQueen.Goal Estêvão (21).Tottenham Hotspur Kinsky, Robertson (Kyerematen, 72; Tingey, 90+1), Davies (Takai, 81), Van Hecke (Danso, 46), Gray, Gallagher (Hardy, 54), Tonali (Donley, 81), Bergvall (Hall, 72), Tel (Williams-Barnett, 76), Solanke (Richarlison, 46), Solomon (Moore, 67).Substitutes not used Dubravka, Scarlett, Russell-Denny, Melia, Yang, Ajayi, Byrne, Tye Hall.Booked Gallagher (10).Goals Tonali (17), Richarlison.Sent off Danso (49).

Tottenham’s Premier League campaign begins at Brentford on August 22.

July 28- Western Sydney Wanderers 4 Chelsea 6Today- Chelsea 1 Tottenham 2August 5- Chelsea vs JuventusAugust 8- Chelsea vs AC MilanAugust 9- Johor Darul Ta’z vs ChelseaAugust 15- Chelsea vs Real Sociedad

Chelsea begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham on August 24.

Possession: Chelsea 46%-54% TottenhamShots: 14-7Shots on target: 4-4Corners: 1-1

There is the final whistle and the 10 men of Tottenham snatch victory at the death with Richarlison scoring with seconds remaining.

In the final few seconds of the game, 10-man Tottenham win it. Donley’s shot from just outside the box hits the post and Richarlison follows up to score. It would have been a close call on offside if VAR was in use but it is not and Tottenham will take victory in Sydney.

Tottenham are being forced into a late change as Kyerematen, who come on for Robertson and nearly scored that wonder solo goal, is being forced off injured and is replaced by Tingey.

Delap is found in the centre of the Tottenham box with a cross from the right but the striker’s header from around the penalty spot goes wide and does not really trouble the target.

Initially, after Danso’s red card, Chelsea were in the ascendancy with a man advantage but Tottenham have dealt pretty well down a man.

Kyerematen nearly scores a quite sensational solo goal from inside his own half before driving forward. As he approaches the Chelsea penalty area, he tries to pick out the top corner and his effort comes off the top of the bar.

Xabi Alonso is making seven changes, yes seven, at once! That includes the likes of Delap and Tosin, who takes the captain’s armband.

The changes keep coming as Williams-Barnett replaces Tel for Tottenham.

A reminder that if the game is level after 90 minutes there will be a penalty shoot-out.

Roberto de Zerbi is making a double substitution as Tye Hall and Kyerematen replace Bergvall and Robertson.

17-year-old Satpaev, who hails from Kazakhstan, is replacing Estevao for Chelsea. Satpaev, who was at Kairat and turns 18 in 11 day’s time, scored the other day for Chelsea against Western Sydney.

Moore, who was on loan at Rangers last season, is replacing Solomon for Tottenham.

Robertson is so, so lucky. He is under no pressure as a cross comes over from the left and he should clear it with ease. However, he tries to be too clever and chests it back looking for his goalkeeper. There is not enough on it, allowing Pedro to nip in but his effort from inside the six-yard box is saved. Pedro probably should have scored and Robertson is a relieved man. Kinsky at the moment is the reason why Tottenham are not a couple of goals behind.

Tottenham have found it tough to get forward a lot since Danso’s red card but they do counter now and it ends with Tonali having a shot from just outside the box but his effort is easily saved by Sharman-Lowe.

Chelsea make a change as Anselmino comes on for Hato.

Palmer plays a ball down the right channel to pick out the run in behind of Palestra, who then returns it back to Palmer inside the Tottenham penalty area. Palmer’s first-time effort from the edge of the box is blocked.

Kinsky makes another big save to deny Chelsea. Tonali, who thought he had been fouled, loses the ball deep inside his own half, before Estevao has a great chance to put Chelsea in front from inside the Tottenham penalty area but Kinsky makes the save. It would have been a touch soft to give a free-kick to Tottenham but in the Premier League you suspect Tonali would have been awarded a free-kick there.

Tottenham are going to make a change at the back in light of Danso’s red card. Hardy is going to come on for Gallagher, who is booed by some of the Chelsea fans inside Accor Stadium. The England Under-18 international Hardy has come on at right centre-back in place of Danso.

Chelsea hit the frame of the goal. Pedro cuts it back from the byline to the penalty spot. Estevao gets to it first and his shot takes a deflection off Robertson. Kinsky makes a brilliant reflex save to push it onto the bar before Colwill blazes over.

Roberto de Zerbi is slumped in his seat distinctly unimpressed, shaking his head in frustration and perhaps disgust.

Palmer takes the free-kick but his effort is always curling wide of the far post.

The Austrian defender came on at half-time but has lasted just three minutes before being given his marching orders. Danso makes an absolute mess of a pass back to him from Gray and lets the ball run past him. Pedro gets around him and looks destined to drive towards the Tottenham penalty area but is brought down. Danso is shown a red card as Davies was probably not going to get across in time and it was the denial of a goal-scoring opportunity. Why do that in a pre-season friendly? Stupid.

Tottenham are making two changes at the break as Richarlison and Danso come on for Solanke and Van Hecke. Chelsea have also made a substitution as 16-year-old Nicoll-Jazuli comes on.

It appears the more times you see the incident involving Wesley Fofana and Conor Gallagher right at the end of the first half the more it looks like a penalty. Fofana did not appear to get the ball and instead catches Gallagher so Tottenham can probably feel a little aggrieved not to be given a penalty.

What have you made of that first half? Remember you can share your thoughts and opinions in the comments section at the bottom of the blog.

Possession: Chelsea 31%-69% TottenhamShots: 3-3Shots on target: 1-2Corners: 0-1

The first half is brought to an end and it is level at 1-1 at the break in Sydney.

Should Tottenham have been awarded a penalty? Robertson whips the ball in from the left to pick out the run of Gallagher into the box. Gallagher appeared to get to the ball ahead of Fofana, who seemingly then took Gallagher out but the referee does not point to the spot. That was a risky challenge to say the least from Fofana and on first viewing probably should have result in a penalty.

Palmer plays the ball forward to pick out the run in behind of Pedro, who has a two-on-one with Kinsky but the offside flag quickly goes up. Pedro was miles offside.

That was a decent opportunity for Tottenham. Tel finds the underlapping Davies with a pass towards the byline and the latter plays it across the six-yard box but Solanke was not there to meet it. Had Solanke read that, it would have been a simple tap-in.

Tel comes close to putting Tottenham back in front. It would have been a great solo goal as he drives inside from the left wing and moves into the Chelsea penalty area. He gets the better of Essugo on the corner of the six-yard box but is denied by a decent save from Sharman-Lowe.

Pedro has a chance to put Chelsea in front but his effort goes wide. Chelsea steal possession inside the Tottenham half after a poor pass from Robertson and the ball is then played forward to Pedro, who shoots from just inside the Tottenham box but his effort goes wide of the far post. Davies did just enough to put Pedro off.

Tottenham have two penalty appeals in quick succession turned down. First was for a potential handball by Essugo and then a push by Palestra on Tel. The handball would have been very harsh and the second incident was never a foul on Tel, who was losing his balance anyway.

Chelsea gift possession away deep inside their own half and Tel’s eyes light up. The ball rolls across to the Frenchman in a central position just outside the box and he opens up his body, trying to curl one into the top corner, but gets his first-time effort all wrong and his shot misses the target by a mile.

Like London buses, two goals come in quick succession and Chelsea are back on level terms. Chelsea counter from deep inside their own half and the ball ends up with Gittens on the left. From the corner of the box, he crosses towards the far post. It takes a touch off a Tottenham defender and ends up at the back post where Estevao, one of the smallest men on the pitch, beats Robertson and heads into the opposite corner.

Tottenham take the lead in Sydney courtesy of £100m signing Tonali. Solomon lays it back to Tonali who, from just outside the box, hits it first time and his shot takes a big deflection off Colwill, taking it into the far corner and giving Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal no chance. That was probably Tottenham’s first proper foray forward in the game.

It has been a pretty stop-start game as play continues to be halted by fouls. The two managers might enjoy seeing the passion of their teams but they will also want to see their sides actually play, which is quite difficult when fouls are being committed left, right and centre.

Van Hecke has already fouled his former teammate Pedro once and he bundles into him again. Van Hecke has a wry smile as he walks away and Pedro tells the referee that is now twice he has been fouled by Van Hecke. I think it is a fairly safe assumption that Van Hecke and Pedro do not like each other that much!

We are not even 10 minutes into this friendly but there is absolutely no love lost between these two sides and the challenges are flying in. Former Chelsea man Gallagher slides in on Essugo, which infuriates the Chelsea players. The referee takes his time to make his decision as both sides come to blows before giving out the first booking of the game to Gallagher.

Pedro is caught by Van Hecke out on Chelsea left and the latter is absolutely furious with that decision, believing he got the ball. However, replays show that he did not get the ball and a free-kick was the right decision. Those two were teammates at Brighton and supposedly were involved in a training ground altercation just over a year ago!

The free-kick is whipped in towards the back post and the last touch is deemed to have come off Chelsea, much to their chagrin.

Lavia catches Tonali late and eventually the referee blows his whistle to bring play back for the free-kick. In a Premier League game, that may well have been a booking for Lavia. It might be a pre-season game but there will be no love lost between these bitter rivals.

The pitch in Sydney is on the bobbly side, which will make slick passing more challenging, dare I say it probably not really possible or realistic.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel, with Tottenham led out by Archie Gray and Chelsea by Levi Colwill. There is a lights show inside Accor Stadium as the teams making their way onto the pitch.

Roberto de Zerbi has indicated Tottenham are not done bringing new players in.

“My summer was great. I had seven weeks off or something, which I’ve never really had. I went on holiday with my family and I feel fresh. I didn’t know where to go. I went on holiday and I was thinking ‘where do I go next?’ I kept checking when I was back in. To be fair, I got bored in the sixth week. I was sat in Marbella thinking ‘I want to go back’ and I’ve never thought that!

“The first few months of me being injured, I just wanted to go out and play, which I probably shouldn’t have done as I couldn’t play how I wanted to play. I went to Sweden or Denmark to see a doctor and we did speak about surgery, but I didn’t end up getting it. It was a bad season, personally, with injuries and stuff, but I feel good now. Seven weeks off obviously helps, but I’m ready to go again.”

Mykhailo Mudryk, the Chelsea winger, has been cleared to return to competitive football with immediate effect after the anti-doping case against him was resolved.

Mudryk has not played for Chelsea since November 2024 after he tested positive for meldonium, a banned substance.

The Ukrainian has consistently insisted that he never knowingly used the substance and that he did not understand how it had entered his system.

“I think two, maybe three [more signings]. We have to see. Bomba in Italian is different from bomba in English. You can write what you want, no problem, no pressure. But I said we have to complete the transfer market. I think we have some other players to complete the squad, and the players will be here in the next few days; for me, they are top players.

“I do not know if the expectations are bigger than two days ago, but we have to go forward and think of the good of the team, of the club, of the squad. But in Italian, it is a different word. I think Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Senesi, Robertson are bomba. For me, top player for us.”

Chelsea have avoided a points deduction for making off-the-books payments during the Roman Abramovich era, but have been fined £10m and given a suspended two-window ban on signing players.

Chelsea’s punishment follows an investigation into 74 alleged breaches of the Football Association’s regulations regarding agent, intermediary and third-party payments.

It has now been revealed that Chelsea were initially punished with a six-point deduction, suspended until June 2027, but successfully appealed against that sanction.

It is a Premier League encounter Down Under as Chelsea take on Tottenham at the 82,000-capacity Accor Stadium in Sydney. Chelsea won both meetings in the league last season, winning 1-0 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium before a 2-1 victory at Stamford Bridge in the final few weeks of last season.

It is the start of a new era at Chelsea, with former Bayer Leverkusen and Real Madrid midfielder Xabi Alonso taking over. They began their tour down under with a crazy 6-4 win over Sydney Wanderers, with Joao Pedro scoring a hat-trick. Chelsea have broken the British transfer record to bring in Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa. Rogers is not on this tour as he enjoys time off following England’s World Cup exploits, with the likes of Reece James, Enzo Fernandez and Malo Gusto also not involved.

It has been a busy week for the club off the pitch as they secured the signing of French centre-back from Maxence Lacroix from Crystal Palace and are closing in on deals for both Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson. Chelsea’s opening game of the new Premier League season will be a west London derby as they travel to Craven Cottage to take on Fulham.

Tottenham have already played two games on their tour down under. A 2-0 win over Auckland FC in New Zealand was followed up by a 1-1 draw against Sydney FC on Wednesday. Tottenham have been very active in the transfer market this summer. In particular they have targeted Premier League players including Andy Robertson, Sandro Tonali and Jan Paul van Hecke. Mohammed Kudus, Xavi Simons, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert have remained in the UK as they continue their rehabilitation from injuries.

Goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario has also stayed at home with a minor knock but the Italian has been linked with a move away from Tottenham this summer. Djed Spencer, Pedro Porro and Cristian Romero are not on the tour following their World Cup exploits. They begin their Premier League campaign with a London derby as they take on Brentford at the Gtech on the opening weekend.

#2084. West Ham Have Hired A Championship Specialist – And I’m Delighted

A lot has already been written about incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker, and I make absolutely no apologies for being excited about his appointment.

To be crystal clear, Parker probably wouldn’t have been my first choice. But I’d reached the conclusion that Nuno Espírito Santo was incapable of taking West Ham forward, and with the club desperately needing to revive its Championship promotion campaign, a change was essential.

Is Scott Parker capable of doing that? Absolutely. As Claret & Hugh has confirmed through its own sources at West Ham, Parker is set to become the Hammers’ new head coach. And I believe there are two particular qualities that could make him exactly what this team needs.

I understand there are reservations about Parker’s record in the Premier League, and perhaps even the football his Burnley team played during their most recent promotion campaign.

After all, Burnley had the meanest defence in the Championship, and some supporters are understandably concerned that West Ham might be replacing one cautious manager with another.

But far from viewing that defensive record as a negative, I’d suggest West Ham desperately need somebody capable of improving our back line.

We’ve looked disorganised defensively for far too long, and a manager who can actually get players defending properly would be a welcome change.

Espirito Santo could not fix West Ham’s defence

Not that I want us to be boring, of course.

I also believe Parker is capable of getting more out of the players in attack, particularly the likes of Jarrod Bowen, Divine Mukasa and Lewis Orford.

And there’s something else worth remembering.

Parker has achieved promotion from the Championship with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley. Three promotions with three different clubs.

That’s not a bad record for somebody being brought in to do precisely the same job at West Ham.

I’m often reminded of something former Blackburn Rovers manager Mark Hughes said about signing striker Roque Santa Cruz.

Hughes explained that he’d watched the player countless times but decided to concentrate on what he could do rather than obsessing over his flaws.

It’s something that has always stuck in my mind.

And I think it’s particularly relevant when assessing Parker.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on his shortcomings, I’d prefer to focus on two qualities that I believe could make an enormous difference at West Ham.

Parker is an infectious character and a motivational speaker. He’s somebody who communicates with passion and conviction, and I believe that alone could make a considerable difference to this squad.

In short, I think he’s a far better communicator than Nuno Espírito Santo.

That might sound like a relatively small thing, but I don’t believe it is.

West Ham have looked like a team lacking confidence, direction and motivation for much of this season.

A manager who can get his message across clearly and make players believe in what they’re doing could transform performances without changing a single member of the squad.

One of my biggest frustrations with Espírito Santo was his apparent inability to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to football matches.

Time and again, we’d begin games slowly, allow opponents to take control and then spend the rest of the afternoon trying to recover.

It was a problem Nuno repeatedly acknowledged but never seemed capable of fixing.

And I suspect motivation played a significant part in that.

Whatever else people might say about Parker, I find it difficult to imagine his players routinely wandering onto the pitch looking half asleep. He’ll have them fired up, motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle.

Of course, enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to win football matches.

But Parker also has the tactical experience to back it up.

He’s demonstrated that he understands the Championship, knows how to organise a team and can put together a successful promotion campaign.

I certainly don’t expect him to be out-thought tactically by virtually every opposition manager, which increasingly appeared to be the case under Nuno.

And while there will undoubtedly be questions about how Parker’s methods translate to the Premier League, that’s a discussion for another day.

We’re in the Championship, and our immediate priority is getting out of it.

Scott Parker has already demonstrated on three separate occasions that he knows exactly how to do that.

In short, Scotty P understands this Championship stuff considerably better than Nuno ever appeared to.

And I don’t see too much wrong with appointing a specialist for the job.

#2082. “Scot Will Be There” Parker’s First West Ham Decisions Could Come Within Hours

Claret & Hugh has been informed within the past few moments that incoming West Ham manager Scott Parker is likely to have some input into team selection for tomorrow night’s Championship game against Cardiff City. The former Hammers midfielder is also expected to attend the match, despite Mark Noble being set to take charge on the touchline.

As West Ham confirmed in their official statement earlier today, Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville have been placed in temporary charge of preparations following the dismissal of Nuno Espírito Santo. However, the information we’ve received suggests that Parker could still have a say in the team that faces Cardiff.

A C&H source told us just moments ago: “Scot will be there and he’ll have some influence on the team even if he can’t do all of it.”

West Ham’s final training session ahead of the match took place earlier today at Rush Green, before Parker had even signed his proposed two-and-a-half-year contract. But that doesn’t mean he will have no input at all, particularly with the new manager expected to be in attendance tomorrow evening.

Being something of a Championship specialist, and of course a former Hammer, Parker will already be familiar with West Ham’s form and performances this season. I suspect he’ll also have a reasonable idea of which players he wants in the team and which ones might benefit from a spell on the sidelines.

As Claret & Hugh revealed earlier today, Parker’s proposed contract is closely tied to West Ham securing promotion this season. With that in mind, there is every reason for him to want to influence proceedings as quickly as possible, even if Noble is the man officially overseeing tomorrow’s game.

And, to be perfectly honest, I don’t think Parker needs to reinvent the wheel to make some immediate improvements.

There are a couple of really easy wins available to the new Irons gaffer, and some of them should be blindingly obvious to anybody who has watched West Ham over the past few months.

Morato was Nuno’s first choice left back.

Firstly, a rousing team talk and a little bit of urgency might be enough to address West Ham’s dreadful starts to games. It was a recurring problem under Nuno Espírito Santo, and one the former manager never seemed capable of fixing. Getting the players motivated and ready to compete from the opening whistle would be a welcome change.

Then there’s the fairly straightforward business of putting round pegs in round holes. For starters, let’s play an actual left-back in the left-back position. That alone would immediately improve the balance of the team rather than continuing to ask players to operate in unfamiliar roles.

Finding the right blend in midfield would also be of huge benefit. West Ham have spent far too much time surrendering control of what is arguably the most important area of the pitch, despite having some talented options available. Getting that balance right could make an enormous difference to the team’s performances.

And finally, there’s Jarrod Bowen. Surely one of the most obvious priorities for any incoming West Ham manager is getting our best attacking player into as many goalscoring positions as possible. Bowen has spent far too much time being asked to produce something out of nothing, and a better-functioning team should make his job considerably easier.

Okay, it’s all a bit paint by numbers, and there’s nothing particularly revolutionary or overly tactical about those suggestions. But that’s rather the point.

West Ham’s problems have often appeared so obvious that you wonder why they’ve been allowed to continue for so long. Parker doesn’t necessarily need weeks on the training ground to recognise them, and even a quick word with the players before kick-off might help address some of the most glaring deficiencies.

Of course, Noble will be responsible for managing the team against Cardiff, and there’s only so much Parker can realistically influence before he’s properly taken charge.

But if the new manager can offer a few sensible suggestions and inject a little urgency into proceedings, I’d suggest that would already be a step in the right direction.

#2081. Nuno Ignored the Answer to West Ham’s Defensive Crisis

Nuno Espírito Santo has always been described as stubborn by many players and former colleagues, and his continued reluctance to trust either Soungoutou Magassa or Edson Álvarez was becoming increasingly difficult to understand, particularly as West Ham continued to concede soft goals and struggle to protect their back four.

It is a decision, among others, that ultimately contributed to him losing his job.

The issue is not necessarily that West Ham lack talented midfielders. The problem is balance. Too often, the midfield has looked easy to play through, leaving the defence exposed to direct attacks and transition situations. When opposition teams bypass the first line of pressure, the centre-backs are frequently left defending large spaces with insufficient protection in front of them.

That is where Magassa could be invaluable. A converted central defender, the Frenchman is naturally suited to operating as a holding midfielder. His game is built around positioning, breaking up attacks and providing physical presence rather than driving forward or creating chances.

Álvarez offers a slightly different solution. Throughout his career, he has excelled as a midfield shield, winning duels, intercepting passes and protecting defenders. He has also played at centre-back for club and country, underlining his defensive instincts and tactical discipline. While he may lack the mobility to play in a highly expansive system, his ability to sit deep and screen danger is exactly the kind of profile West Ham have often appeared to be missing.

What made Nuno’s stance particularly puzzling is that both players offer something the current squad lacks: specialist defensive security. When a team is leaking goals, managers often look to simplify things, becoming harder to break down before worrying about attacking fluency. Selecting either Magassa or Álvarez in front of the defence could provide that extra layer of protection, reducing the burden on the centre-backs and limiting the number of dangerous situations they face.

Soungoutou Magassa was reinstated to the West Ham squad.

Of course, Nuno saw these players every day in training and may have valid reasons for excluding them. There have been questions over attitude, tactical suitability or future plans, which may all play a part. However, from the outside looking in, West Ham’s defensive record makes it increasingly difficult to justify leaving two natural defensive midfielders on the sidelines while persisting with approaches that continue to leave the back line vulnerable.

Equally, both players are sitting on the wage bill and not playing. In itself, that’s hard to make sense of.

At some point, results have to outweigh previous decisions. If West Ham are serious about tightening up defensively, Magassa and Álvarez look like obvious solutions hiding in plain sight. The question now is whether the interim management will see it?

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

Then you look at the team dynamic among the group. The players who decided to stay and knuckle down in the championship when they knew that the goal of the club was to keep as many first teamers as possible. The players who tried hard to jump ship at the first opportunity. Players like Mangassa and Alverez who don’t want be at the club. Then what you reward them with a place in the team over and above the players who stayed loyal? Not for me.

#2080. Hearts pay tribute as former captain Don Murray dies aged 80

Former Heart of Midlothian captain Don Murray has died at the age of 80.

The central defender spent almost two years at Tynecastle during the 1970s and captained the Jambos during the inaugural Scottish Premier Division season.

It is with great sadness to announce the passing of former captain, Don Murray, at the age of 80. An iron-hard central defender, Don spent less than two years at Tynecastle, but he made a fine contribution, assisting Hearts to qualify for the initial Scottish Premier Division campaign, as well as reaching the Scottish Cup Final in May 1976. Our thoughts are with Don's family and friends at this time ♥️ A tribute to Don, by Club Historian, David Speed, can be read on our website 👉 https://t.co/2FJZwVWGfT

— Heart of Midlothian FC (@JamTarts) November 3, 2026

Hearts announced that Murray died on Monday at Llandough, near Cardiff, and paid tribute to a player who made 71 appearances for the club.

The club said: “It is with great sadness that the club learned on Monday of the death of former captain, Don Murray, at Llandough, near Cardiff. He was 80 years of age.”

Born into a farming family at Duffus, near Elgin, in January 1946, Murray began playing with Hopeman Junior School before progressing to junior football with Burghead Thistle.

He signed for Cardiff City in January 1963 and went on to become an influential figure at the Welsh club.

Murray made 527 appearances for Cardiff and helped them reach the League Cup semi-finals during the 1965-66 season and the European Cup Winners’ Cup semi-finals two years later.

His performances also earned international recognition with Scotland at under-23 level.

After a brief loan spell at Swansea City, Murray joined Hearts for £15,000 in December 1974.

Don Murray (Image: Colorsport / Shutterstock)

His arrival helped bring stability to a difficult campaign as Hearts secured their place in the newly formed Premier Division for the following season.

Murray was subsequently appointed captain and led the Jambos during that historic first Premier Division campaign, when they finished fifth.

Hearts also reached the Scottish Cup final in 1976, although Murray was denied the opportunity to lead the team out against Rangers at Hampden because of a calf injury.

He remained captain for the club’s subsequent tour of Norway and Australasia, but continued to struggle with the injury at the beginning of the following season.

Murray left Hearts for Newport County in October 1976 after making 71 appearances for the Edinburgh club and later played for Barry Town.

Following his retirement from football, Murray worked as a social worker.

Hearts added: “Don always led by example.”

The club extended its condolences to Murray’s family and friends following his death.

#2079. Time to admit Newcastle United have made a huge mistake, no not that one

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Is it time to admit that Newcastle United have made a huge mistake?

“Any man can make mistakes, but only an idiot persists in his error” – Marcus Tullius Cicero

After another shocker of a Newcastle United performance against Everton last night, there is a growing anger and frustration in the fanbase with the direction (or lack of) of the team on field.

Consistent underperformers, no clear strategy, and players proven not to be good enough are selected regardless, though to be fair, managing to be toothless up top as well as all over at the back is impressive.

The knives are sharpening for Matthias Jaissle and he’s looking to be all mouth and no trousers. But for me, appointing Jaissle, isn’t the biggest mistake we’ve made in the last year or so, that dubious honour goes to the appointment of Ross Wilson (pictured at the top with David Hopkinson).

You might think and say well Wilson actually had a pretty decent CV, on paper it looks good, he was involved at Southampton when they brough Van Dijk in, was at Rangers when they broke Celtic’s grip on the SPL and was at Forest when they stayed up and then qualified for Europe.

Delve a bit deeper though and Rangers fans tend to give credit to his predecessor and are still trying to get rid of some of his flops and elsewhere while he’s had successes his overall recruitment strategy is scattergun at best. Theres no clear player type of strategy picked up, very opportunistic and he’s got good players at good prices (particularly getting Anderson from us) but it seems the strategy is slinging a lot at the wall and seeing what sticks.

If you look back since the takeover we’ve had two highly thought of Directors of football come in and go not long afterwards due to ‘issues’ with others at the club, so despite having a reasonable CV he didn’t come in with as big a reputation and to this observer his primary attribute was he was affable to Eddie and his nephew, which at the time made some sense as Eddie had put together an all time season in 24/25 and looked like he’d be our manager for years to come even after that summer of 25.

So Ross Wilson came in after that summer, which now with the benefit of hindsight has been nothing short of disastrous, with Elanga, Wissa and Ramsey being total overpays (as well as two of them debatably being our biggest wastes of money ever) and Woltemade being a glass slipper when we needed a steel toe capped boot.

Of course, we can’t put any of that on Wilson as he didn’t join till afterwards and it would be a challenge for even the best directors of football to deal with the fallout of it all.

The first warning signs for me came in the January 26 transfer window, when the team was on the ropes, Eddie was struggling and we didn’t bring in any first team recruits to assist a struggling squad. Now I know some of you will bring up the likes of PSR, FFP, SKY 6, Ashley, the Illuminati as reasons why we didn’t spend, but even one signing could have reinvigorated the squad and at least limited the late season slide we went on.

The risk is we’d have to sell at the end of the season to cover ourselves but we had to sell in any case because we plummeted down the league and didn’t even get any European football in one of the weakest Premier Leagues I can remember. It showed very little foresight for Ross Wilson to sit on his hands when the team was visibly on the ropes.

We then come to the end of the season where we have plummeted, put together some Bruce level performances and lost another derby which allowed our dear rivals to experience Europe for the first time in a lifetime. The performances were so poor and we looked totally bereft of ideas. Eddie Howe looked a shell of the man who’d once had us putting it up anyone we came up against.

The decision was there to be made, all logic pointed to a departure of a club legend but as Eddie Howe didn’t quit, Ross Wilson didn’t make the decision to let him go. There’s always the loyalty argument but at that stage it was just ignoring the evidence your eyes presented to you to keep him.

This eventually backfired as by mid pre-season Eddie took the decision out of his hands and left for some well-earned rest and relaxation. This put us further on the back foot as a lot of managers had already moved at the end of the previous season and we’d already started our season’s preparations expecting Eddie Howe to be our manager.

The next managerial move was to bring in Matthias Jaissle, who talked one hell of a game, got to give him and the club credit as the way he was presented looked amazing and had most of us very excited for the potential but then the football started. The ‘vertical football’ promised turned out to be an Allardyce like hoofball without the defensive solidity and if they’d played Stelios as their CF rather than Davies.

As a toon fan Ive had plenty of opportunity to make judgement on God awful managers and all I can see with Jaissle is another one.

Could Wilson have been duped like the rest of us? Of course he could of, but even if he was his actions with 50m+ in the bank to go and sign a left winger who thinks they are a forward when we needed a proper physical CF, a 10, pacy ball playing CBs and an inverted RW was just negligent. Don’t get me wrong, Matias Fernandez-Pardo could turn out great, but it was such a bad use of resources.

In a similar note the signing of Ewen Jaouen is looking like excess which wasn’t needed, again he could be great but spending eight figures on a back-up goalkeeper is just wasteful at best. Signing a bunch of youngsters for a manager who won’t give them minutes in general is foolish.

Overall, regardless of the many flaws Matthias Jaissle has shown, Ross Wilson hasn’t built a squad that’s fit for purpose for the system that Wilson hired the new Head Coach for.

Looking at what we did on outgoings we can also see issues with the way Wilson worked, our pet media liked to say we are trying to use the Brighton model, ignoring that the Brighton model is to bring in younger players who have time to settle in before selling your bigger names. This year we sold all three of Bruno, Gordon, and Tonali before bringing in replacements, putting us straight on the back foot.

We have different opinions on the value we got for those three players (personally I think we sold too early) but having a replacement ready for none of them just shows Ross Wilson hasn’t prepared properly.

Looking at other decisions made over the summer, giving Harvey Barnes an extension rather than cashing in seems similar to previous decisions not to cash in on the likes of Miggy/Wilson after they’d had hot streaks. Barnes puts up great goals and assists stats, and you’ll get the argument ‘where would we be without his goals,’ but I disagree and think a better all-round player will benefit the team more eventually.

The Palace game is the prime example of what Barnes is, great finish for his goal but the number of attacks of ours that broke down because of his unwillingness/inability to beat a man, poor passing and poor decisions was in double figures. I think he’s an effective sub but the time to cash in was this summer gone.

The worst decisions though were to come and that was the decisions not to take the cash for both Murphy and Willock at the end of the window, the decision just tells everyone in the squad that they are the standard.

Murphy’s hot spell is long in the past, he can put in the occasional good cross (maybe one in three or four) but his all-round games makes Barnes look like the complete winger, he’s often terrified in possession and will put teammates under pressure or just play it to nobody so he doesn’t have it. You can also add his age, so to turn down the claimed £15m transfer fee is ridiculous. You may say ‘but he’s a good presence’ turning down £15m (as well as keeping Premier League wages) for someone who smiles and claps is a bit much. As for NUFC needing options on the right – Elanga, Pardo, Osula, Barnes and Wissa have all played on the right at some point and Joelinton and Ramsey have played on the left.

Joe Willock was an afterthought for Eddie Howe, but to his credit this season he’s popped up with some key goals and his chaotic style seems to suit our headless gameplan a little bit at least, though to turn down whatever transfer fee could have been banked in the summer is a failure in long-term squad building.

Overall, we may not quite be a sinking ship just yet due to riding our luck so far, but we can’t continue to go on like this. To fire Matthias Jaissle without also firing Ross Wilson would be like getting rid of the monkey without the organ grinder, so we need to remove Wilson from his position too, to try and get back on the right track.

I’m sure some will say you need to give directors of football time, but sometimes when something is wrong you just need to bite the bullet and move on, rather than persisting with the mistake.

#2078. Rafa Benitez or Sean Dyche to replace Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle United?

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

So then, who is it to be, is it Rafa Benitez or Sean Dyche to replace Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle United?

No, Newcastle United haven’t got rid of their Head Coach, at least not yet.

Although clearly there appears to be plenty of Newcastle United fans who would like that to happen. Today, if not earlier.

There is though of course only one small problem.

If Matthias Jaissle was to leave, then Newcastle United would need a new Head Coach.

It is all very well screaming for the man in charge to go but you have to then have a succession plan.

Yes, I know that wouldn’t be your job, your are just a fan, but careful what you wish for.

Having a look at what happened last season, maybe it is little wonder that as yet, Matthias Jaissle and the other 19 Premier League managers remain in their jobs still in 2026-27.

In total, eleven Premier League managers were sacked during last season (with their replacements in brackets), with seven of the Premier League managers to be sacked during the 2025-26 season exiting from only three clubs!

9 September 2025 – Nuno leaves Forest (Ange Postecoglou) 27 September 2025 – Graham Potter leaves West Ham (Nuno) 18 October 2025 – Ange Postecoglou leaves Forest (Sean Dyche) 2 November 2025 – Vitor Pereira leaves Wolves (Rob Edwards) 1 January 2026 – Enzo Maresca leaves Chelsea (Liam Rosenior) 5 January 2026 – Ruben Amorim leaves Man U (Michael Carrick) 11 February 2026 – Thomas Frank leaves Spurs (Igor Tudor) 12 February 2026 – Sean Dyche leaves Forest (Vitor Pereira) 29 March 2026 – Igor Tudor leaves Spurs (Roberto de Zerbi) 22 April 2026 – Liam Rosenior leaves Chelsea (Caretaker boss for rest of season) 30 April 2026 – Scott Parker leaves Burnley (Caretaker boss for rest of season)

The ridiculous Forest owner actually got in even quicker this time and sacked the manager (Pereira) before this 2026-27 season even started! Their fifth manager in less than 14 months, Oliver Glasner, currently only has Sunderland to thank for keeping him and Forest off rock bottom.

Oliver Glasner of course was somebody that so many Newcastle United fans were thinking would be a great choice for NUFC not so long ago.

Well I suppose at least we won’t need to wait too long before Glasner is back on the market judging by the way the Forest owner happily swings the axe.

Seriously though, who would Newcastle United get if they moved Matthias Jaissle on in the near future?

I hear Newcastle United fans saying that it was obvious that in the summer NUFC shouldn’t have gone for somebody who has no Premier League experience.

Well just have a look at what happened last season as I have listed above, so many managers with Premier League experience getting hired and fired.

If Matthias Jaissle was sacked, I think Sean Dyche or similar would be the kind of Premier League experience that would be available and keen on the job.

Sean Dyche was dismissed by Everton on 9 January 2025 when they were only one point above the relegation zone, having only won three of their last nineteen games in the 2024–25 season.

On 21 October 2025, Sean Dyche was appointed as manager of Nottingham Forest and lasted less then four months, Dyche sacked in February 2026 having won six of his 18 Premier League games in charge at the City Ground and Forest fourth bottom.

Rafa Benitez is another name I have seen mentioned.

Nobody loves Rafa Benitez more than me and he deserves our everlasting love and respect for what he did when the evil on owned Newcastle United. He gave us hope when there was none and did a brilliant job.

The curse of NUFC appears to have drained his magic though.

The managerial career of Rafa Benitez has been a total car crash in the seven years since Mike Ashley forced him out.  Disasters at Dalian Professional, Everton, Celta Vigo and Panathinaikos. Not quite the career progression that preceded Newcastle United, when Rafa went Valencia, Liverpool, Inter Milan, Chelsea, Napoli, Real Madrid…

The idea that Rafa Benitez would suddenly rediscover his magic wand if returning to St James’ Park is simple fantasy, though not fantasy football.

This isn’t to say that Matthias Jaissle shouldn’t be sacked, he hasn’t got a job for life.

However, to only give him nine Premier League matches after he walked into a club in total chaos 18 days before the season kicked off.

Well, it isn’t my idea of a clever move and that is even before you begin to look at the very likely potential replacements.

#2077. ‘It’s a bit of a pity for Nick Woltemade, Matthias Jaissle is a fantastic coach…’ Christian Ziege

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Christian Ziege has been talking about Nick Woltemade and Matthias Jaissle.

The former Bayern Munich and Germany defender looking ahead to what could be possible at Newcastle United.

Nick Woltemade had an up and down first season with United in the Premier League and the three other competitions.

A lot of the media going way over the top with criticism, as the inexperienced striker still scored 11 goals and got a number of assists across the 2025-26 season.

The German international striker saw Eddie Howe leave in the close season and Matthias Jaissle arrive only 18 days before the 2026-27 season kicked off for NUFC.

Matthias Jaissle left Big Nick on the bench for the 2-2 draw with Liverpool and then the striker played the full match as United won 3-2 against West Brom in the Carabao Cup.

Nick Woltemade then came on with 20 minutes to go and Newcastle United leading 1-0 at Tottenham, within a minute Big Nick had got an assist as Wissa made it 2-0 and ensured the away win in the Premier League.

The decision though was then taken for Nick Woltemade to spend the rest of this season on loan with Juventus, as Matias Fernandez-Pardo was signed.

Christian Ziege declaring to Boyle Sports: “I hope Nick Woltemade returns to play under Matthias Jaissle at Newcastle. It’s a bit of a pity for Nick Woltemade, Matthias Jaissle is a fantastic coach who proved himself in Austria and Germany. Woltemade is another example of a player who had one good season at Stuttgart before moving straight to Newcastle and it looks like it was too soon. Performing consistently for three seasons before a big move is very different from moving after just one. The Premier League is tough for strikers, and things didn’t quite work out for him there.”

No doubt many people reading this will wonder two things.

Will Nick Woltemade ever return to play for Newcastle United instead of being sold?

Whilst if Big Nick did ever play for United again, would Matthias Jaissle still be the NUFC Head Coach by that point?

Christian Ziege: “Now Nick Woltemade is on loan at Juventus and Serie A can be even tougher for strikers. Perhaps he should have stayed to work under Jaissle at Newcastle, but if he returns from loan to work with him later, it could be a different story. Let’s hope that everything is going in the right direction for both Woltemade at Juventus and then maybe later for Newcastle.”

After getting very limited chances early on at Juventus, Nick Woltemade has now started five games in Serie A and the Europa League with Juventus winning four of them and drawing the other. Big Nick scoring three goals and getting one assist so far.

#2076. Andoni Iraola wishes Alexander Isak had done one thing differently in Liverpool defeat

Andoni Iraola is convinced that Liverpool would ‘100%’ have been awarded a penalty on Sunday if Alexander Isak had gone to ground after having his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber.

The Reds’ head coach was left bewildered over that incident in the 21st minute of the Reds’ 1-0 defeat at home to Arsenal, for whom Kai Havertz had scored just five minutes earlier.

Neither Andy Madley nor the officials on VAR duty felt that a spot kick was warranted, a decision which was met with unified disagreement from Jamie Carragher, Ian Wright and Daniel Sturridge on Sky Sports.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola felt that the incident was a ‘clear penalty’ and believes that a foul would’ve been given had Isak gone down when Timber pulled his shirt.

The Liverpool boss said: “The fact that you are even asking me that he should have gone to the floor, that’s the thing. If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty for me. They call the penalty 100%.”

When the interviewer asked the Basque whether he’d tell Isak to go to ground if that happens again, he replied: “Yes, definitely.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

We now have a farcical situation whereby Iraola feels compelled to openly advocate for his players to go to ground under contact from opponents because the officials on duty are failing in their task.

Quite frankly, Isak shouldn’t feel any obligation to engineer a penalty in such situations, seeing as the shirt tug from Timber was so blatantly obvious that there’s no justification for those on VAR not to intervene, whatever about the on-field referee missing it.

It’s the striker’s job to try and get on the end of the ball coming into the box (which he probably would’ve done if his jersey wasn’t pulled), not to seek the manufacturing of a spot kick because the officials can’t be trusted to do their job of calling such clear fouls.

That decision felt significant in the overall context of the match yesterday. Had the referee awarded the penalty as he should’ve done, Liverpool would’ve had a chance to quickly cancel out Havertz’s goal.

Had they done so, we can’t help but feel that it would’ve been a rather different game at Anfield. Obviously that’ll forever remain hypothetical, but there’s a real sense of what might’ve been had the officials not erred so badly over the incident involving Isak and Timber.

#2075. Unseen moment Rangers star warned 'job's not done' by team-mate after semi-final win

Ivor Pandur delivered a stern warning to one of his Rangers team-mates after advancing to the final of the Premier Sports Cup.

The goalkeeper was caught telling Findlay Curtis to cool his celebrations at Hampden as he insisted the 'job is not done'.

Rangers posted a clip on social media of the players leaving the park in Glasgow after Ryan Naderi's late goal sent them through to the final. Rangers will face Hibernian next month.

🤩 Full-Time Scenes at Hampden! 💙 We're heading to the Final!! https://t.co/zOlCkZ6aKW

— Rangers Football Club (@RangersFC) October 31, 2026

And while the players were understandably jubilant as they were greeted by coaching staff and club staff as they left the park, Pandur wasn't allowing anyone to get carried away.

Curtis was passing the camera when he let out a loud celebratory cheer. Pandur then stepped in to motion to the young Scotland winger to calm down.

Pandur could then be seen and heard saying: "Easy bro, job is not done, bro."

After leading Rangers into the final, Derek McInnes commented: "I'd like to have enjoyed it a wee bit more. Enjoyment comes now, to be honest, a wee bit of satisfaction when I see the lads in the dressing room celebrating together.

"But the job now is to go and win the thing, and we'll get six weeks now between now and then where we need to get better at things I just spoke about.

"The players who are in the team at the minute need to play well to stay in the team if they want to be in the cup final, and the players who are not in the team need to keep performing and doing all they can to get in the team.

"We need to drive each other on because we want to get into the cup final on the back of some really strong league form.

"We're on a really strong run just now in terms of wins and being unbeaten over a period of time now. But we know we're not perfect.

"It's important that we keep searching for those improvements. But if we can keep winning, keep putting ourselves in cup finals and keep ourselves satisfied with results, we can keep working on performances."

#2074. City fire blanks in shoot-out as Maresca’s opening game ends in defeat by Inter

Manchester City lost the Asahi Super Dry Trophy 3-1 on a penalty shoot-out against Inter Milan.

Enzo Maresca took charge of the Premier  League runners-up for the first time since his arrival as Pep Guardiola’s replacement, though he was without many of his stars who had yet to return from World Cup duty.

One of the players missing was Elliot Anderson, the £116m signing from Nottingham Forest, though Jeremy Monga, 16, was an unused substitute after being brought in from Leicester City in the summer transfer window.

City took the lead on 14 minutes through Divin Mubamba as he tapped in an Antoine Semenyo cross, but Inter’s experienced defender Benjamin Pavard levelled just six minutes later when City failed to clear a corner.

The Premier League side dominated possession in the second half after an even first 45 minutes but could not find a way through. Phil Foden, the captain, was again underwhelming after a difficult year last season, but with the season still to come he had plenty of time to show his best form once more after signing a new contract at the Etihad.

The game went to penalties after full-time with no extra time played, and only Claudio Echeverri held his nerve for City as Inter Milan scored three of theirs, Matteo Lavelli netting the winning spot-kick.

Both teams learnt little from the match as Inter made 11 changes and City eight, though Maresca will have been impressed by Ryan McAidoo’s performance as a second-half substitute, as he regularly threatened from the right wing. The 18-year-old forward will surely be in demand from other clubs looking to loan him, and City may yet be tempted to keep him around for the coming season.

Manchester City Donnarumma; Lewis, Khusanov, Gvardiol (Reis, 46), Mfuni (Alleyne, 46); Kovacic (N González, 46), Reijnders (Ait-Nouri, 46); Savinho (Braithwaite, 78), Foden (Echeverri, 68), Semenyo (Sangare, 68); Mubama (McAidoo, 46).Substitutes not used Bettinelli, Wint, Chabot, Monga, Mukasa, F.
